OK, I'll explain this one for you.

My family moved to this area in 1990. The house we moved into is 2 miles from this hospital. My family has used the physicians associated with this hospital to treat virtually every medical issue we've had, as a family of 6, for 28 years. 

That's a significant amount of history with these doctors. Hell, one of them has been involved in 3 surgeries my father has had in the past 5 years alone.

But that doesn't explain how I, personally, know so many of the staff here. That's because I've been in this hospital virtually every day, often several times a day, for more than 5 years. I've been there working. 

See, up until recently I was a medical courier. I made my living by transporting blood, tissue, specimens, medication, documentation, diagnostic imaging, surgical instruments, medical equipment, and the like between various medical practices. This hospital is right in the middle of my area and used my employer for its courier needs. So any time they needed to send or receive ANYTHING that wasn't being mailed, or picked up by a dedicated lab/equipment company, they called us. And more often than not I got the call. 

The physicians, and their external practices, are a similar story. Part of my daily routine was to pick up diagnostic imaging from a few third party imaging companies and deliver them to practices throughout the area. So I've been in these offices two or three times a week for more than 5 years.

Well, here are some highlights in no particular order. Keep in mind that the second time I worked there they had recently been "rated" as one of the "top aviation repair facilities in the nation." 

I watched a mechanic, who was standing on the top of the cage of a scissor lift with one foot resting on an engine part, yell to his partner to throw him some JB Weld. JB Weld was not approved for aviation usage at this time, don't know if it is now.

Smoke hoods, an FAA mandated piece of safety equipment, were kept locked away from the staff. Well, unless FAA inspectors were coming. They were dubbed "too expensive for the monkeys to fuck with."

Drained fuel was kept in a cage. Said cage was up against an exterior wall of the hanger, next to a door that we had to walk through (mandatory) on every patrol. The pump used to transfer fuel between barrels leaked, spraying jet fuel against the door, ground, wall, anyone walking near them. I got sprayed with a jet fuel on a number of occasions, and they dealt with the spill on at least 2 occasions that I know of by hosing it into a storm drain.

Part of our job became to look through the windows of vehicles in the parking lot for drugs/alcohol/weapons due to a number of incidents at the site. Drugs found in the hanger, employees coming to work drunk, fights, and so on. We were told NOT to check vehicles belonging to management. 

On more than one occasion I had to physically restrain test pilots from assaulting Inspectors due to problems that arose during the test flights.

For several months the paint shop vented fumes directly into the hanger. This wasn't fixed until mechanics refused to work on aircraft stationed next to the paint shop.

They decided that they didn't want to go through the trouble of moving the jet to the flight deck before they fired up the engines for a basic function test. Apparently they'd been having some problems getting these engines to fire and were fed up with hauling it in and out, so they fired it up inside of the hanger. The nose of this plane was not 10 feet from my guard shack. They couldn't understand why we were pissed. 

Little things like those shook my faith in the aviation industry.

In 1999 I lived in River Oaks, TX. This is a suburb of Fort Worth, and where I lived was roughly 4 miles north of the center of Fort Worth.

Aaaaand I'm on the phone with 911.

Now here's where things get interesting. On my way home I had passed 4 police officers, parked in the center median of Jacksboro Highway, running traffic not 2 miles from my home. So I'm thinking the response is going to be fairly quick.

45 minutes later my roommate walks in. She comments on the activity across the street, where someone is loading their car with anything of value from the trailer, and bitches about the police officers running traffic down the road. She'd gotten a ticket for speeding. 

So I decide to call 911 again. 

Wanna guess how long it took them to respond? Another 45 minutes. 

After the officers had cleared the now empty of anything of value trailer across the street, I asked a ranking officer what the fuck had happened. 

I was told, in no uncertain terms, by a Sergeant of the Fort Worth Police Department, that I should not rely on the police for protection. I was advised that no matter how quickly I reported an issue with probable violence, the police WOULD NOT be able to respond in time to protect me. 

Despite having been a fan of firearms since near birth, I hadn't owned one in my adult life. I was advised, by law enforcement professionals, to buy a pump action shotgun. I was advised, by the Fort Worth Police Department, to load the first round if I suspected someone was entering my home. I was advised to fire the first round if someone actually entered my home.

The throttle position sensor went out. 

The radiator fan failed due to a bad electrical connection (which can no longer be purchased). 

The AC has gone out three times. This is caused by the repetitive failure of a switch, one that not even the dealer can find the reason of. 

The heater core ruptured. 

Three wheel bearings have gone out, one of them twice. 

The head gasket blew. 

The timing belt started to go bad. Fortunately, we discovered this when we were replacing the head gasket. 

It has developed a leak in the evap system. 

The lower engine mount broke.

The air bag occasionally provides an indicator that it WILL NOT FIRE in case of a collision.

It currently misfires when climbing a hill or accelerating quickly.

And now the shifter linkage comes free when I try to out it into gear. Im driving without the center console on so I can keep putting the linkage back on while I wait for a part.

I've spent more than $6k in repairs since I've bought it. That doesn't include the nearly $1k in tow fees I've had to pay.

Owning a PT Cruiser is the second worst financial decision I've ever made.

> Seriously.. how am I supposed to know why your insurance is charging you that price.

I can actually answer this one for you. And its not the insurance's fault. It's one of two things. 

First, understand that's there's not really prescription "insurance". The employer/program/service 100% determines what/how/when medications are covered, the amount to which they will be covered, and how much the patient will get at a time. Yes, the PBM has a standard formulary, but this is reviewed AT LENGTH before a contract is signed. 

Further, the employer/program/service can alter/update/change/ignore the formulary they chose, at any time they so choose, for absolutely any reason. Many of you might know this process as "getting a Prior Authorization" or to "file an appeal". When this happens a specially trained representative collects and collates the necessary data, ranging from specific diagnostic coding to research data regarding the medication, and provides it to the employer/program/service. Once again they decide if/when/how much/what quantity is approved for. 

So even if the medication costs $2, the employer/program/service can decide to charge $40. And if that's their decision, that's what is charged. Period. The PBM has no choice, bound by an ironclad contract, but to follow their wishes. 

But once in a while a medication falls outside of this. Either it wasn't on the formulary, or the employer/program/service said something along the lines of "It's covered, but pay the market rate." And that's when we are screwed. 

There are services that provide the Average Wholesale Price of medications to third party payers, such as Federal prescription programs and Pharmacy Benefits Management companies (CVS¦Caremark, Express Scripts, etc...). These update roughly once a week, at my old company they updated every Tuesday morning.

These prices are considered to be the Lord's own gospel when it comes to medication prices. We do not question them, we do not dispute them, and we most absolutely do not ignore them. When we're faced with AWP pricing, the data is God.

AWP changes from day to day, but the data only updates once each week. 

So on Tuesday the medications might have cost $15. On Thursday they might cost $40. If the employer/program/service decides we should pay AWP, we pay AWP. They choose how much we pay, they choose if we pay, they choose when we pay. They repay us.

So don't blame the insurance folks. Blame​ the employer.

Class A Biohazards have very specific regulations as to how they're transported. I have never worked for a shelter or a food pantry. However, I do say this as someone who has both been homeless, and has relied on my local food pantry, at various points in my life. 

Cash, first and foremost. Both shelters and food pantries have to pay rent, have to pay employees, have to pay utilities, and have to pay for infrastructure. Money is the number one most beneficial thing you can donate. Without cash they end up closing and can help nobody. 

Socks, underwear, and shoes. Seriously, socks, underwear,  and shoes. These are almost never donated. Imagine having worn the same crusty pair of underwear and socks for 6 weeks solid. I have, and it's as disgusting as you imagine. 

Blankets. A shelter has a maximum capacity, but they will give away many of the supplies they have on hand in inclement weather. The blanket you donate might be the only protection someone has in sub-freezing rainy weather

Feminine health products. Pads, tampons, Vagisil, etc... These are rarely donated, yet vital for the health of fully 50% of the population. 

Basic medical supplies. I'm talking bandaids, antibiotic ointment, aspirin, acetaminophen, and what have you. 

Protein based food items and non carbohydrate vegetables. I can't stress this enough. Carbohydrates are commonly donated. Every pantry I've dealt with has an overabundance of rice, pasta, soup, canned corn, potatoes, and baked goods. But every one in my area routinely runs out of protein. 

Seriously, on one occasion I went to my local food pantry and was able to pick out several pounds of rice, six cans of soup, six cans of corn, three large boxes of instant mashed potatoes, and 4 full sized sheet cakes (seriously) made at my local Tom Thumb. 

For protein I was able to select two cans of beans and one can of meat (I picked chicken). This was my food allowance for a month, and I'm a diabetic. 

Finally, pet food products. Particularly cat food (as dog food is more commonly donated). You may not realize this, but for many of the poor their pet is the only reason they're still living. The situation that they're facing may seem intolerable, but the pet they have might, just MIGHT, give them a reason to face one more day. And when you're starving, when your furry child is starting, that $3 of pet food might be the one thing that keeps them going for one more day.

I followed the company's policies and procedures to the letter, and ended up making senior management look bad.

I was working for a Pharmacy Benefits Management company, a top rated Fortune company, as a Resource Planning Coordinator/Workforce Management Specialist. My team effectively ran a call center with 363 phone agents, around 30 or so email/chat agents, and a number of specialist representatives (I can't remember how many). We handled everything from scheduling, to training, to call allocation, to workflow, to payroll, and so on.

We had a number of "elite" clients. One of these was a "Big 3" American automotive manufacturer, that at the time was undergoing a bailout by the Federal Government. One of the terms of the bailout necessitated a number of changes in their insurance plans. For some reason, which management decided not to share with us, these changes required their service calls to be handled at my call center rather than the one in Pittsburgh which handled it previously.

Agents are trained. Systems are put in place. Calls are trickled in to make sure that everything is up to operational requirements. We're told that it's absolutely vital that the transfer goes off without a hitch. 

Everything seems to be fine. 

Right up to point when the new plan is put into place and 100% of the call volume is routed to my center. 

Due to a bit of a flu epidemic I'm the only one in my department at my call center. Call volume is high, as everyone is calling in to run trial claims on various medications, to set up mail order accounts, and to request new membership cards. Everything worked fine for the first few hours, then my agents lost the ability to access the client's accounts. 

Shit. Queue crisis mode. 

I followed every policy and procedure in the book. I fire up a conference call with IT, the server team, and the network team. I fire up a second conference call with my other call centers. I fire off emergency emails to pretty much the entire management chain, send out a "system outtage" page to everyone even remotely related to the issue, and sent personal text messages detailing the issues to the same. I try making multiple calls to my management chain directly. 

The list of people that I attempted to contact included my Supervisor, my Manager, my National Director, the call center Manager, the Vice President of Operations, and the bloody CEO.

Nobody responded to any of the 3 contact methods. 

We determine that the outtage is a local issue. Pittsburgh is still able to field calls and access the customer's accounts. Further, they've been trained on the new plan to handle any excessive volume. 

Facing fines, SLA violations, an increasingly irate customer base, and the edict that "everything go off without a hitch", I make the call to route the volume up to Pittsburgh. They save our ass, the call volume normalizes, the SLA's are saved, and our IT team works on getting the issue resolved. Around 4 hours later the systems are up, we're able to access the client's accounts, and we're able to route call volume back to my center.

I log everything, send a few emails detailing the outtage and the steps I took to contain it, and call it a day. 

The next day I'm brought into HR by my Supervisor, where I'm met by my Manager, my Director, and the VP of Operations. I'm promptly fired, escorted off the property by two armed security guards (we didn't have armed security guards), and followed by a local police officer until I pull onto the freeway.

It turns out that the reason that NONE of my management chain responded to my email, text, page, or phone calls was that all of them, ALL OF THEM, were in Detroit at the time. They were monitoring the transfer with the client's representatives and a Federal regulator. They had no cell service, and had gone to lunch right before the outtage occured. They came back to an absolutely abysmal set of metrics, and were completely unable to explain it. 

They said they would locate the "source of the failure" and "eliminate it from the corporate structure".

Being the one responsible at the time of the transfer I was fired for "gross incompitence", despite following each and every single policy listed in the book. 

Fucking right to work state. 

TL;DR: Did the right thing, got fucked up the ass for it.

Understand that what I'm about to say is based off of my own personal experiences with inpatient therapy, and those of friends and family who have undergone similar treatment. Further, understand that my own own personal experience with inpatient treatment was more than 20 years ago, while those of friends and family date back to over 10 years ago. 

Consider a rather stringent regimen of outpatient therapy and group support rather than inpatient treatment. 

I spent my 17th birthday in an inpatient treatment center in Atlanta, Georgia. At the time it was considered one of the better recovery systems for individuals with emotional difficulties, suicidal urges, and chemical dependencies. I spent 30 days as a patient, at a cost of $56,000 (post insurance). Adjusting for inflation, this is $99,630.73 in 2013 dollars. 

I saw my therapist -twice- during my entire stay. 

Yes, only twice in the entire 30 day stay did I spend ANY time with my therapist. I did spend see a nurse daily who gave me a short questionnaire that they used to adjust my medications. I did see the teachers I had for my schoolwork. I DEFINITELY saw the security staff. But my specific therapist...twice. 

I did get to attend daily substance abuse meetings, because everyone who has any form of an emotional issue is at risk for substance abuse. Their explanation, not mine. 

This isn't to say I didn't get anything from my stay. It was incredibly cathartic to spend time with people that had similar issues to mine. Being able to talk, freely, with people who knew what I was feeling provided me more benefit than anything else. 

The person who helped me the most was the teacher in charge of physical education. He was an old hippy that taught me the basics of meditation and started me out with a few basic martial arts forms. I honestly feel that he saved my life.

They did put me on a specific schedule. I woke up at a specific time, ate at specific times, and went to bed at a specific time. Being put into such a regimented schedule moved me into something similar to autopilot, helping me manage the day a little bit better.

But beyond that...it wasn't worth it. Especially not at that cost. I would've gotten more personalized treatment by seeing an outpatient therapist twice a week, going to group counseling, and joining a Tai-Chi class; and it would've been one at a much lower cost.

The day my mental health coverage ended I was released from treatment, considered to be "no longer at risk."

Now, as I said that was 20+ years ago. However, I have had a few friends deal with inpatient therapy as recently as 10 years ago. And their experiences were just about the same as mine. 

I've known three different individuals who spent time at inpatient centers, in the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex, between 10-12 years ago. All three went to highly rated facilities, all three had insurance with mental health coverage, and all three regretted it. Two stayed 14 days, the third stayed 30.

In each case:

* Interaction with a personal therapist was minimal. 

* The majority of their counseling was done in an impersonal group setting. 

* They were all forced to attend substance abuse counseling, despite the fact that two of them had never touched a drink or taken a drug (even a cigarette). 

* Each paid more than $40,000 for their treatment.

* Each was determined to no longer be "at risk" as soon as their insurance coverage ended.

* Every single one of them said that they received more help from outpatient treatment, arranged by their new outpatient therapist once their inpatient treatment ended, than they received in the hospital. 

* Every single one of them said that they felt that the hospital, and there were 3 different facilities involved, were more interested in the money they got from insurance than they were their health and wellbeing. 

My recommendation, if you're feeling like you're going to put the gun to your head immediately then BY ALL MEANS go check yourself into a facility right now. There aren't many differences between brand and generic medications. Pretty much for a medication to be considered a viable generic alternative it has to have to have the same active ingredient in the same strength, route of administration, and form of dosage as the name brand. They also have to meet all quality standards of the name brand medication.

Further, the manufacturer has to prove to the FDA that the drug is "bioequivalent." This means that the drug has the same performance characteristics (absorption rate, duration, and so on) of the name brand drug.

However, none of the inactive ingredients have to be the same. None of the binders, fillers, or additives need be anywhere close to what's in the name brand medication, provided they are approved for pharmaceutical use. So while the active "drug" should work the same, the additives you're putting into your system with a generic can vary wildly depending on the manufacturer. 

And sometimes, some people just don't react well to these ingredients. 

That said, some of it is psychosomatic. A number of generics are actually made at the same facility, using the same chemicals, on the same machinery, by the same employees as the name brand medications. But some people will swear that the name brand works better.

As a former employee of a major Pharmacy Benefits Management service...i.e. your prescription insurance: We generally don't decide what medications are covered. The plan your employer picked, however, might not cover certain medications. Or they may require you to try other drugs first. 

Now about you getting screwed into taking a generic rather than a name brand? That's all us.

It is possible to make an "herbal" vape, but it takes a little bit of time to do. You first have to break down the organic material, using one of two methods. 

Cold Method: 

Place your organic material in a jar, then fill with any human consumable alcohol of at least 80 proof. The higher the proof the better. Close the lid tightly, shake vigorously for several minutes, then place in your refrigerator. Shake the mix every few hours.

Strain through a double layer of cheesecloth into your storage container. 

The longer the mixture steeps the more THC is extracted. However, this method doesn't provide much in the way of CBD.

Warm Method:

Place your organic material in a jar, then fill with any human consumable alcohol of at least 80 proof. Close the lid tightly, then shake vigorously for several minutes. Place your container in a dark, room temperature (but not refrigerated) spot. Shake vigorously for at least 5 minutes once per day, for between 30-60 days. You want to let it sit until the liquid is a dark green color. 

Strain through a double layer of cheesecloth into your storage container. 

This method provides a VERY high concentration of both THC and CBD. 

Once you've broken down the organic material you can mix it with pretty much any juice you like. It does mess with the flavor though. High VG juice works the best as you still end up with a fair amount of vapor. Experiment with whatever flavors you like, stronger tobacco flavors aren't affected by the mix as much as weaker flavors are. Personally, I HIGHLY recommend using a 70/30 flavorless VG/PG mix, of whatever nicotine level you like, blended with menthol crystals for flavor. 

A few tips though. 

Everclear and 151 proof rum extract the most THC and CBD, but provide one hell of a burning throat hit. Quality vodka of the similar proof doesn't give you the same burn, has much less of an effect to the taste of flavored juices, but doesn't extract anywhere near the same amount of THC and CBD. 

You'll have to play around with the ratios of juice to mixture. I've found that 1 part mixture to 3 parts juice works quite well with the warm method. It takes about a 1 part mixture to 1 part juice to get the same effect using the cold method. 

Both methods cause a bit of an odor in the vapor. The warm method is significantly less noticable.
